narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors in your profile. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. While accepted students typically rank around the middle of their class, you placed in the second decile, signaling consistently lower performance relative to your peers. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 also worked against you; it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were admitted. These two academic signals together created a clear picture of elevated risk.

Your family income, listed as Middle, was the only factor that slightly favored success. Middle-income applicants make up about 35% of accepted students, so this background is fairly common among those who succeed. However, its positive effect was not strong enough to outweigh the academic concerns.

In short, the combination of lower class standing and GPA outweighed everything else, leading the model to conclude your likelihood of passing the bar on the first try was too uncertain for admission.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on raising your academic performance where possible, consider retaking the LSAT to improve that score, and look for post-baccalaureate or preparatory programs that can demonstrate stronger readiness before reapplying. (218 words)
